title-group.article-title: Aligning MRI and CBCT for Advanced TMJ Diagnostics: Case Series Using AI-Powered Registration in Dentistry and Orthodontics

abstract.p: This study demonstrates the functionality and clinical value of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) registration using a new open-source artificial intelligence (AI) model called MR2CBCT. We present five clinical cases in which the AI-based method was used to register CBCT and MRI images. For comparison, manual registration was also performed. Qualitative inspection revealed that manual alignment often showed errors that could compromise diagnostic accuracy. In contrast, the AI-based approach consistently corrected these discrepancies, producing more anatomically coherent fused images to better support clinical decision-making. Our findings highlight MR2CBCT as a reliable and accessible tool for multimodal integration in temporomandibular joint (TMJ) assessment in orthodontics and general dentistry.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The advent of three-dimensional imaging has brought profound advancements to both medicine and dentistry. Among the most impactful technologies are Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), each offering detailed visualization of anatomical structures from complementary perspectives. CBCT is particularly effective for assessing hard tissues and has become increasingly utilized in dentistry over the past decades, especially for pre- and post-surgical evaluations by oral and maxillofacial surgeons1–2. More recently, its diagnostic potential has also been recognized in orthodontics2–3, where enhanced spatial accuracy can improve treatment planning and outcome assessment.

MRI, by contrast, provides high-resolution imaging of soft tissues2,4–7, While it allows for the visualization of hard tissue, this can prove challenging to clinicians. MRIs have been predominantly used in medical contexts. However, its relevance in dental practice has grown significantly, particularly in the management of temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disorders, where soft tissue integrity plays a critical role in diagnosis6.

Despite the distinct advantages of each modality, no single imaging technique currently enables simultaneous three-dimensional visualization of both hard and soft tissues in a clinically convenient form. This limitation is clinically significant in conditions such as TMJ degeneration, where pathological changes may affect both the bony structures of the mandibular condyle and the soft tissues of the articular disc, since it proves extremely challenging for clinicians to fully capture these interrelated changes by analyzing only one of these image modalities, multimodal registration becomes a valuable diagnostic tool6.

To address this, researchers have proposed multimodal image integration, wherein CBCT and MRI scans of the same patient are superimposed using a stable anatomical reference 9–12. While conceptually straightforward, this process is technically demanding: differences in head positioning, imaging geometry, and the complexity of MRI interpretation make accurate registration difficult for most clinicians.

It is important to note the many challenges when integrating two different imaging modalities, particularly, voxel and slice sizes and difficulty with different fields of view (FOV) between these modalities can make registration particularly challenging.

Differences in voxel size and slice thickness are major complications8 since voxel-based registration Is one of the most reliable ways to superimpose an image, recently these issues have been circumvented by utilizing robust registration models, these are models that rely on intensity independent methods like Mutual information instead of merely trying to match voxel for voxel, one of the prime models utilized is Elastix9,13.

So far, there is a limited number of studies that address the use of MRI and CBCT integration in clinical research 9–12, some suggesting good accuracy for superimposition while others remain skeptical. This is expected, since only relatively recently robust registration models have become available to address the issues of voxel size, slice thickness, and other factors. But now that this integration is possible, it becomes fundamental for clinicians and researchers to consider utilizing this new method of analysis

Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful ally in overcoming these challenges by automating parts of the image registration process. Recent developments from our group include a novel open-source multimodal registration module integrated into the 3D Slicer software platform named MR2CBCT, described in detail in this study. It offers clinicians an accessible way to fuse CBCT and MRI data, potentially enabling more comprehensive diagnostics and advancing individualized standards of care in orthodontics and beyond9.
Therefore, this study aims to present the clinical application using 5 cases of a recently developed open-source artificial intelligence tool to assist clinicians, called MR2CBT.

sec.title: Materials and Methods
sec.p: This pilot study aimed to present a novel multimodal image registration tool (MR2CBCT) recently developed by our research team using artificial intelligence algorithms on an open-source platform called 3D-slicer14. The study was granted exemption by the University of Michigan Institutional Review Board (IRB HUM00239207), and the requirement for informed consent was waived.

The MR2CBCT tool was developed by the Dental and Craniofacial Bionetwork for Image Analysis (DCBIA). Technical details regarding its development can be found at 9. This paper will showcase five cases to better understand what clinicians can achieve with this tool. Figure one shows a small guide with images from the 3Dd Slicer software to assist clinicians with utilizing this tool.

sec.title: Imaging Protocol and User Guide
sec.p: The software 3D slicer14, version 5.9.0 (https://download.slicer.org/) was used for all of the processing steps cited.
The steps for using the tool MR2CBCT are as follows:

sec.label: I)
sec.title: Imaging Pre-Processing
sec.p: Before utilizing the MR2CBCT module, clinicians must ensure that the “Automated Dental Tools” extension is properly installed, as MR2CBCT is integrated within that suite. Next, both the CBCT and MRI scans must be saved in NIfTI format.

sec.label: II)
sec.title: CBCT orientation and segmentation
sec.p: The CBCT should be oriented and segmented before registration. This can be done using the commands in the “Pre-Processing” section of the MR2CBCT module (Figure 1) or through other tools within the Automated Dental Tools extension15. For orientation, the ASO module is recommended, while segmentation can be performed using either the AMASS or BatchSegmentator models.

sec.label: III)
sec.title: MRI pre-processing and image cropping
sec.p: For MRI pre-processing, clinicians should use the section immediately below the CBCT pre-processing area (Figure 2), which allows for MRI orientation and centering. While manual adjustment of the orientation guidelines is possible, the default settings provide reliable alignment in most cases. It is essential to crop both the MRI and CBCT scans to focus on the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) region, as this is the primary area of interest for the model. Cropping can be done using the command box located below the MRI pre-processing area (Figure 3). Alternatively, clinicians may use the “Auto Crop 3D” module from the Automated Dental Tools extension, which allows them to define a custom bounding box for image cropping.

sec.label: IV)
sec.title: Resampling
sec.p: With the oriented and segmented images, clinicians can proceede to the resampling step, which is fundamental for making sure both the CBCT and MRI have the same parameters, which makes registration possible. The “resampling” command box is the one above all other boxes (Figure 4)

sec.label: V)
sec.title: Approximation
sec.p: Once all pre-processing steps are complete, the clinician can proceed with image registration. The first step is to perform an initial approximation, found below the pre-processing section (Figure 5). The clinician must select the folders containing the cropped and oriented MRI and CBCT scans, then click the “Approximate” button. This step helps align the two datasets by correcting large angular and linear discrepancies, making accurate registration possible.

sec.label: VÎ)
sec.title: Final Registration
sec.p: Following approximation, the clinician should move to the command box below the approximation step (Figure 6). Here, they must select the folders containing the MRI, CBCT, and the previously obtained CBCT segmentation. The clinician can then configure the normalization parameters, a critical step that ensures the intensity profiles of both scans are compatible for registration. While customization is possible, the two default normalization options are generally suitable for most cases. When all steps are completed, the registered image is saved in the output folder specified by the clinician.

sec.title: Registration Based on Artificial Intelligence and Imaging Processing
sec.p: The parameters and protocols employed by our AI model are comprehensively described by Leroux et al.9 This model provides users with an automated pipeline that integrates AI algorithms with traditional computational methods. Artificial intelligence is utilized by this model to perform image segmentation and orientation tasks. These components are essential, as both orientation and segmentation present significant challenges and are time-intensive processes, particularly for clinicians with limited expertise in medical image interpretation and minimal experience with segmentation software applications.

Additional pipeline components, including centering and resampling (geometric transformations), image cropping, MRI gray-level inversion, and intensity normalization, constitute mathematical, geometrical, and statistical operations. The registration process itself is implemented using Elastix13, with core registration procedures such as mutual information calculation, rigid registration optimization, iterative parameter adjustment, and mask application representing a combination of geometrical, mathematical, and statistical computations.

Nevertheless, all operations performed by this module whether AI-based or traditional computational methods, are imperative for achieving accurate multimodal registration. This hybrid approach leverages the pattern recognition capabilities of artificial intelligence for complex perceptual tasks while employing established mathematical frameworks for geometric computations, thereby ensuring both clinical usability and registration precision.

sec.title: Quantitative assessment
sec.p: The present case series considered both quantitative and qualitative criteria to assess registration quality. Quantitatively, the AI-based model has been previously validated in the literature9, where it demonstrated improved linear and angular alignment metrics compared to manual registration performed by clinical experts using multimodal datasets. This prior validation supports the technical accuracy of the tool used in our case series.

sec.title: Qualitative Assessment
sec.p: Qualitatively, the registrations were evaluated through a structured consensus process among clinical experts based on specific anatomical criteria. Each case was initially assessed by an experienced clinician and subsequently reviewed by additional clinical experts until consensus was reached on registration quality. In the sagittal superimpositions, the evaluators analyzed the relationship between the articular disc, condyle, and glenoid fossa, focusing on potential interpositions or misalignments and how well the disc accommodated within the joint space. In the 3D segmentations, emphasis was placed on coronal and axial alignment (roll and yaw) and the presence of overlapping structures. In the volumetric images, attention was given to the visual congruence of the mandibular condyle with adjacent anatomical landmarks such as the zygomatic arch, coronoid process, and temporal bone. This combined framework enabled a structured clinical interpretation of registration quality while relying on previously published quantitative benchmarks of the AI-based tool.

sec.title: Results and Discussion
sec.p: In the five cases presented (Figures 7-11), we demonstrate the superimposition of MRI and CBCT images focused on the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) region. This multimodal fusion allows clinicians to visualize various TMJ structures more accurately and comprehensively. For example, condylar resorption is more clearly observed in the CBCT scan, as shown in Figure 7. While this finding may be technically visible on the MRI, it would be challenging for most clinicians to identify with confidence. In contrast, the CBCT provides a more distinct view of bony morphology, making the small and altered shape of the condyle readily apparent.

Disk abnormalities, on the other hand, are more effectively assessed using MRI due to its superior soft tissue contrast. Abnormalities in the glenoid fossa are best visualized with CBCT. Key spatial relationships such as those between the articular disk, the condyle, and the fossa require input from both modalities to achieve optimal diagnostic accuracy. In all five cases, patients exhibited morphological or positional abnormalities involving the condyle, articular disk, and/or glenoid fossa. While it may be technically possible to evaluate some of these features using a single imaging modality, doing so would be extremely challenging for most clinicians. This highlights the clinical value and practicality of the MR2CBCT tool in supporting precise, comprehensive TMJ evaluations.

sec.title: CASE I
sec.p: In the first case (Figure 7), we compare the registration outcomes produced by a clinician expert (Panels A-F) and our AI model (Panels G-L). In the grayscale superimpositions (Panels C and H), the articular disk appears slightly more anteriorly positioned in the manual registration (Panel C), while in the AI registration (Panel H), the disk aligns more naturally between the condyle and glenoid fossa. This improved anatomical congruency suggests a more accurate positioning of soft tissue structures by the AI.

When analyzing the segmented models (Panels D and I), the disk in the manual registration seems anteriorly displaced and not properly engaged with the condyle appearing almost to “float” within the joint space. In contrast, the AI registration shows the disk centered and in functional contact with both the condyle and fossa. These differences cannot be fully attributed to segmentation variability alone.

In the 3D volume renderings (Panels E-F and K-L), the manual registration is more difficult to interpret due to the lack of resampling, and the cranial structures reveal a slight upward pitch of the MRI relative to the CT. Meanwhile, the AI registration benefits from automated resampling, allowing better visualization and demonstrating superior alignment, note the better fit on the condyle and coronoid process.
Overall, this case illustrates subtle but clinically significant differences between manual and AI-assisted registration, favoring the model’s consistency and anatomical fidelity in the latter.

Patient 1 presented with frequent headaches and earaches following a single incident in which she opened her mouth and heard a cracking sound in the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). An initial attempt at treatment using a stabilization splint worsened her symptoms. Clinically, she presented with a full dentition, midline drift in both anterior and posterior teeth, Class II Division II malocclusion, limited mouth opening, restricted mandibular translation and rotation, and pain in the face, TMJ, and shoulders.

MRI analysis performed by a radiologist revealed signs of arthritic changes in the condyle and raised suspicions of anterior and medial displacement of the articular disk, particularly at the lateral aspect of the joint. Interestingly, in the AI-based registration and 3D segmentation (J), this pattern of disk displacement becomes much more evident. The disk is shown to be laterally displaced and, in the sagittal plane, anteriorly displaced on the lateral side, consistent with the radiologist’s suspicion but now more clearly visualized.

This case demonstrates the potential clinical value of multimodal fusion imaging. The AI-enhanced 3D visualization allowed for a more definitive identification of subtle displacements that were only tentatively described in the MRI report. In complex TMJ presentations such as this, a multimodal approach could lead to more confident and accurate diagnosis, particularly when radiological findings are ambiguous.

sec.title: CASE II
sec.p: In case II (Figure 8) it is possible to see more slight but still significant differences, when comparing the grey level image superimpositions (C-H) there is a very subtle tilt in the second image that makes it so the disk fits alongside the condyle slightly better, in the first image it is possible to see the disk overlapping with the condyle slightly. This is confirmed when looking at the segmented models (D-J), where in the manual approximation we can note a slight interference between the disk model and the condyle, in the AI registration this cannot be noted, in these models it is also possible to note a more centered disk in the AI registration. In the 3d volumes (K-L) it is possible to see a small downward pitch in the MRI, which makes alignment slightly off, on the AI registration (L) we can note a very good fit around the anatomical reference points, notably the condyle, coronoid process and external acoustic meatus.
This case presents fewer notable changes than Case 1; nonetheless, those changes are still significant enough to influence a possible diagnosis.

Patient 2 presented with severe pain in the TMJ and facial region. She had previously undergone orthognathic surgery due to a combination of maxillary hyperplasia and mandibular hypoplasia. Despite surgery, the mandible still appears retruded, although her occlusal relationship remains functionally stable, albeit with a steep occlusal plane.

Clinical analysis of the left TMJ revealed significant condylar resorption and increased vertical joint space. This is clearly visible in the imaging, particularly in (H), where the condyle appears severely resorbed, especially in its middle-lateral portion. A prominent dark space between the disk and the articular fossa further supports this.

The clinician noted difficulty identifying the disk, which is a common challenge when relying solely on MRI. The dark borders of the condyle and fossa can obscure soft tissue structures like a thinned or reabsorbed disk. However, in the fused image (H), the spatial boundaries of the joint are much clearer, allowing for better visualization of what appears to be a posteriorly positioned and likely reabsorbed disk.
This case demonstrates how multimodal registration enhances diagnostic certainty, particularly in joints with complex anatomical remodeling.
This is a case where multimodal integration could have made diagnosis significantly easier for the clinician.

sec.title: CASE III
sec.p: Our third case (Figure 9) presents another example of the improvement of the condyle-disk relation by the AI model registration, in the grey level image superimpositions (C-H), it is possible to visualize that on the manual registration (C) there is overlap of the disk with the anterosuperior part of the condyle, It is also possible to see that the disk seems to be pressing against the posterior and inferior part of the condylar head. Suggesting a mixture of linear and angular misalignments, while in the AI registration (H) it is possible to visualize a much smoother integration, where the disk sits comfortably between the condylar head and the articular fossa. In the 3d models (D-J) it is possible to visualize that in the Manual superimposition (D) the disk tips laterally, seeming to almost detach from the condyle laterally, suggesting excessive roll, and it is also possible to see the disk pressing against the anterior portion of the condylar head, suggesting excessive pitch. Meanwhile, on the AI registration (J) we can see a more harmonious fit on the condylar head. On the 3d volume rendering, it is difficult to visualize the manual registration (E-F) however, specially looking at the frontal view there is distinguishable pitch affecting alignment, meanwhile on the AI registration (K-L) we can see a good fit, especially in the condyle, coronoid process and external acoustic meatus, it is also possible to visualize muscle strands descending the temporal bone. Considering the anatomical position, it is likely that we are visualizing a part of the temporal muscle.
In this case, we can see that although clinicians tend to focus more on the sagittal view, yaw and roll can be just as significant in disrupting appropriate alignment.

Patient 3 reported severe headaches, TMJ pain, ear discomfort, and occasional vertigo. Despite these symptoms, her occlusion appeared functionally stable, with only minor anterior crowding in the lower arch. Clinically, her soft tissue profile suggested anteroposterior skeletal deficiency of both the maxilla and mandible, though this was not prominent on CBCT analysis.

Initial TMJ assessment by the clinician noted mild sclerosis on the superior surface of the condyle and raised suspicion of anterior disk displacement. However, the exact position of the disk remained unclear.

Upon reviewing the fused MRI-CBCT data, we observe distinct anatomical features that clarify the diagnosis. There is marked flattening on the superior surface of the condyle and, notably, additional flattening along the lateral condylar walls (J). The disk does not appear to be anteriorly displaced in this sagittal slice, but instead shows signs of medial displacement, which would have been difficult to confirm using sagittal MRI alone.

This case highlights how multimodal image fusion can uncover subtle spatial changes, such as lateral or medial shifts, that may elude traditional single-modality interpretation. Such findings have direct relevance for accurate diagnosis and treatment planning in complex TMJ presentations.

sec.title: CASE IV
sec.p: Our fourth case (Figure 10) presents a fascinating challenge. Here, we observe that the position of the condyle varies slightly between the CT and the MRI. This discrepancy is likely due to slight patient movement during the MRI acquisition, which is understandable given that MRI scans are longer procedures and can be difficult for some patients to remain completely still. However, even in such cases, regional registration can still yield meaningful alignment.

In the grey-level superimpositions (C and H), the manual registration (C) shows a slight interposition between the disk and the articular fossa. In contrast, the AI registration (H) displays a clearer and more distinct outline between the articular fossa and the disk, indicating a superior fit.

In the 3D models (D and J), the manual approximation reveals that the disk seems to disengage from the condyle posteriorly and encroach upon the boundaries of the articular fossa. On the other hand, the AI registration presents a more harmonious interaction between the disk and condyle, with no visible interposition, suggesting a more anatomically plausible relationship.

In the volume renderings (E-F and K-L), a slight upward pitch is noted in both manual and AI registrations. This is likely an adaptive tilt to compensate for the mismatch in condylar positioning between the two imaging modalities. Despite this, the AI-based volume rendering shows a coherent and continuous alignment of the zygomatic arch and condyle, reinforcing the notion that successful regional registration was achieved despite anatomical variability.

Patient 4 presented with limited mouth opening, biweekly headaches (described as pressure “behind the eyes”), clicking sounds in the TMJ, arthritis in the knees, and severe jaw pain. She characterized the TMJ pain as “a pain that makes me want to cry,” with symptoms aggravated by chewing and yawning. In response, she adopted a soft diet and regularly used ibuprofen and Tylenol for relief. Interestingly, she noted that as her mouth-opening range decreased, the TMJ clicking became less frequent.

A clinical MRI analysis by a TMJ specialist indicated that the condyle was in centric relation, the disk was anteriorly displaced, and the disk appeared macerated, although no significant effusion was observed.

In our fused multimodal analysis (G–L), signs of condylar resorption become more evident. In sagittal view, a distinct dent can be seen on the anterior surface of the condylar head. The disk appears anteriorly displaced, potentially adapting to fill the irregularity left by resorptive change. Furthermore, the disk shows clear signs of thinning and surface damage, particularly on its anterior aspect, consistent with maceration.

This case illustrates how multimodal integration can not only confirm clinical impressions but also deepen understanding of intra-articular dynamics, providing a more nuanced view of structural degeneration in symptomatic patients.

sec.title: CASE V
sec.p: Our final case (Figure 11) underscores the importance of analyzing axial and coronal views with the same rigor as sagittal slices. In the grey-level registrations (C and H), the manual approximation (C) presents a less defined interface, with overlapping regions between the condylar head and articular fossa. In contrast, the AI-based registration (H) demonstrates a smoother and more consistent integration of the disk, condyle, and fossa.

In the 3D segmentations, attention to the coronal plane becomes essential. In the manually approximated model (D), the disk appears to protrude anteriorly, as if “escaping” the anatomical region, and there is a clear tipping of the disk, suggesting roll. Meanwhile, in the AI-registered model (J), the disk maintains a more harmonious relationship with the condyle, without aggressive angular deviations.

The 3D volume renderings (F-L) further illustrate this difference. In the manual registration (F), the overlay fails to conform accurately to the mandibular contour, particularly along the lateral ramus and gonial angle. In contrast, the AI registration (L) shows a precise and stable fit across multiple landmarks, including the condyle, coronoid process, and zygomatic arch.

This case reinforces a critical principle in TMJ imaging: high-quality registration depends on multi-planar consistency. Even minor rotational distortions can compromise anatomical interpretation, and AI registration methods can offer greater stability and reproducibility across dimensions when such variability is present.

Our final patient presented with severe TMJ pain and significant functional limitations. She described extreme difficulty in eating, noting that chewing causes intense pain. To cope, she cuts food into small pieces or relies on liquid alternatives. She also reported pain radiating to the back of her neck and behind her eyes, along with habitual teeth grinding. A bite splint prescribed for sleep has been uncomfortable and disrupts her rest. Previous interventions, including massage therapy and chiropractic treatment, were ineffective. She has not yet attempted physical therapy.
An MRI was requested by the clinician to assess her TMJ condition. Expert interpretation noted condylar degeneration, slight anterior positioning of the condyle, and minimal effusion.

Upon review of the AI-enhanced multimodal images (G-L), several findings stand out. There is notable condylar resorption, particularly along the anterosuperior and lateral surfaces, giving the condylar head a more triangular appearance. The articular disk shows clear anterior displacement, appearing to protrude away from the condyle in the closed-mouth position, a pattern consistent with internal derangement and likely disc-condyle incoordination.

In this final case, we once again observe how 3D fusion imaging not only confirms clinical suspicion but adds precision to the characterization of intra-articular structures. For patients with complex, persistent pain and inconclusive therapeutic responses, such enhanced imaging can be pivotal for redefining treatment strategies.

sec.title: POTENTIAL FOR FUTURE STUDIES IN ORTHODONTICS
sec.p: Combined multimodal imaging analysis could greatly benefit other orthodontic interventions, such as mandibular advancement. Very few studies have explored the positional changes of the condyle in relation to the articular disk and surrounding structures. Among the limited literature available, most studies have been conducted on animal models16, while human studies have typically relied on a single imaging modality17. The integration of CBCT and MRI now allows for detailed, minimally invasive evaluations in human subjects.

This advancement opens the door to new investigations into how the articular disk responds when the condyle is propelled out of the fossa including how long it takes for the disk-fossa relationship to reestablish itself after functional advancement. Additionally, future research could explore whether different functional appliances or advancement protocols (e.g., single-step vs. gradual advancement) produce distinct effects on the delicate environment of the temporomandibular joint.

sec.title: AI in Orthodontics
sec.p: Beyond multimodal registration capabilities, artificial intelligence presents numerous opportunities for enhancing orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning. Within the “Automated Dental Tools” module, several AI-powered functionalities are available, including “AREG,”18 which enables CBCT superimposition; “AMASS,”15 which facilitates automated CBCT segmentation; and “ALI,”19 which provides landmark identification within CBCT scans. Additionally, the DocShapeAXI model19 enables automatic classification of airway restriction due to adenoid hypertrophy20, our research team has developed an open-source, comprehensive, patient-specific prediction model for temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis progression.21 Existing AI models have also demonstrated utility in traditional cephalometric evaluation, with recent studies indicating acceptable performance, though they continue to require clinician validation for clinical implementation.22 Similarly, advancements in AI-assisted panoramic radiograph analysis have shown promise, particularly in models designed to detect periodontal bone loss, which demonstrate effective pathology identification despite inconsistent performance across datasets that necessitates caution and close clinician supervision.23 These represent significant recent advancements in the integration of artificial intelligence and dentistry, with future developments potentially including automated classification of skeletal growth patterns, prediction of cases suitable for fixed mechanotherapy,24 and osteoporosis screening from panoramic radiographs among other exciting and clinically relevant innovations that promise to advance diagnostic capabilities and treatment planning precision in orthodontic practice.

sec.title: Generalizability
sec.p: This case series illustrates the clinical applicability of our AI-based registration model. While its quantitative performance has been previously validated in the literature9, the effectiveness of the CBCT-MRI registration process in practice may still depend on factors such as image quality, the clinician’s adherence to usage guidelines, and the level of care applied during visual inspection of each case. Rather than replacing clinical judgment, the model is designed to augment it, providing a consistent, automated foundation upon which individualized evaluation can be performed.

sec.title: Study Limitations
sec.p: The current study has several limitations that must be considered during interpretation. First, the sample size remains limited, which may affect the generalizability of our findings. The retrospective nature of this study introduces inherent biases associated with historical data collection. While the pipeline is largely automated, the 3D integration and segmentation processes still require some degree of human interaction for optimal visualization and integration of both CBCT and MRI models into a unified view. Finally, the inherent complexity of MRI interpretation presents a significant challenge for general dentists who may lack specialized training in magnetic resonance imaging analysis.25

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This pilot study presents MR2CBCT, an open-source multimodal registration module designed to integrate MRI and CBCT images within the 3D Slicer platform. By enabling accessible, semi-automated fusion of soft and hard tissue data, the tool addresses a critical gap in clinical imaging workflows, especially in the context of temporomandibular joint evaluation. As demonstrated, this platform allows clinicians to extract richer diagnostic information, potentially improving treatment planning for complex craniofacial cases.

caption.p: User interface of the preprocessing module in the MR2CBCT extension. In this step, the clinician selects a folder containing the CT scan and specifies an output folder where the processed files will be saved.
Orientation and centering module of the MR2CBCT extension. The user uploads a folder containing the MRI scan and defines an output folder. The tool reorients the MRI to standard anatomical axes.
Cropping module of the MR2CBCT extension. This tool automatically crops both the MRI and CT scans to the TMJ region, simplifying subsequent processing.
Resampling module of the MR2CBCT extension. The clinician can adjust slice number, voxel spacing, and file size for both scans, or use default parameters optimized for TMJ analysis.
Approximation module of the MR2CBCT extension. This step performs an initial linear and angular alignment between the CT and MRI scans to facilitate later registration.

Registration module of the MR2CBCT extension. After selecting the CBCT and MRI folders and a CT segmentation, the user sets normalization parameters. The tool then performs voxel-wise refinement for accurate fusion.

Multimodal superimpositions of CBCT and MRI scans for five patients. Panels A-F show manual registration performed by a clinical expert; panels G-L depict the corresponding AI-based registration. Panels A and G present the original CT scan for anatomical reference. Panels B and H show the corresponding MRI. Panels C and I display grayscale sagittal superimpositions with 50 % transparency for each modality. Panels D and J present segmented 3D models: the CT-based condyle (red), MRI-based disk (green), and CT-based fossa (blue), with 20 % transparency to highlight anatomical relationships. Panels E and K show frontal 3D volume renderings of the fused images, and panels F and L show the same renderings in lateral view, enabling sagittal comparison.
